title: Moshe Sharett — The Journey That Made The Name

Moshe Sharett (Hebrew: משה שרת; born Moshe Chertok (משה שרתוק); October 15, 1894 – July 7, 1965) was an Israeli politician who was Prime Minister of Israel from 1954 to 1955 and Minister of Foreign Affairs from 1948 to 1956. He signed the Israeli Declaration of Independence and was a principal negotiator in the cease-fire agreements that concluded the 1948 Palestine war.

scenes.narration: Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Moshe Sharett — in that order. Moshe Sharett (Hebrew: משה שרת; born Moshe Chertok (משה שרתוק); October 15, 1894 – July 7, 1965) was an Israeli politician who was Prime Minister of Israel from 1954 to 1955 and Minister of Foreign Affairs from 1948 to 1956. He signed the Israeli Declaration of Independence and was a principal negotiator in the cease-fire agreements that concluded the 1948 Palestine war.

The turning point in the life of Moshe Sharett looked like a failure at the time. Beginning in 1933, he headed the political department of the Jewish Agency. He also founded the Jewish Brigade, which fought with the British Army against Nazi Germany during World War II.

Every biography of Moshe Sharett has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. Moshe Sharett was born on October 15, 1894 in Kherson in the Russian Empire (today in Ukraine) to the family of Yaakov Chertok and Fanya née Lev (לב). For two years, 1906–1907, the family lived in a rented house in the village of Ein Siniya, north of Ramallah.

The education of Moshe Sharett happened mostly outside any school. In 1910 his family moved to Jaffa, then became one of the founding families of Tel Aviv. He graduated from the first class of the Herzliya Hebrew High School, subsequently studying music at the Shulamit Conservatory.

What Moshe Sharett wanted at the start and what Moshe Sharett got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. He then went to Istanbul, then the capital of the Ottoman Empire, to study law at Istanbul University, the same university at which Yitzhak Ben-Zvi and David Ben-Gurion studied. He joined the Ottoman Army in April 1916, serving a commission as "First Lieutenant" and worked as an interpreter.

The defining trait of Moshe Sharett was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. After the war, Sharett worked as an Arab affairs and land purchase agent for the Assembly of Representatives of the Yishuv. In 1922, he attended the London School of Economics, worked for the British Poale Zion and actively edited the Workers of Zion.

Those who met Moshe Sharett at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. One of the people he met while in London was Chaim Weizmann. In 1931, after returning to Mandatory Palestine, he became the secretary of the Jewish Agency's political department.

The private years of Moshe Sharett explain the public decades better than any speech. After the assassination of Haim Arlosoroff in 1933 he became its head. During World War II, via his wife Zipporah, Sharett became embroiled in the question of emigration of refugee Jews stranded in Europe and the East.

The family Moshe Sharett came from matters more than the legends admit. Some Polish refugees, children with and without parents, were deported to Tehran with Soviet agreement. He met with Tel Aviv-bound Hungarian Jewish refugee representative Joel Brand, who had just arrived from Budapest.

The first real success of Moshe Sharett arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. The Yishuv leadership mistrusted Brand, and the British thought him a criminal. Sharett's response was to hand Brand over to the British authorities, who drove him to prison in Egypt.

The last chapter of Moshe Sharett was written long after the fame. Sharett's General Zionism was deeply concerned about making Palestine a commercially viable homeland; its secondary concern was the deep emotional impact of the murder in the Diaspora, which, by 1942, was in German hands. Like Weizmann, whom he admired, Sharett was a principled Zionist, an implacable opponent of fascism, and a practical realist, prepared to co-operate fully with the Mandate authorities.

The whole life of Moshe Sharett reads like a single decision repeated. Sharett, as Ben-Gurion's ally, denounced the Irgun's assassination squads on December 13, 1947, accusing them of playing to public feelings. Sharett held the foreign policy post under the Jewish Agency until the establishment of Israel in 1948.

Between the birth and the legend of Moshe Sharett lie the years that actually decide it. Sharett was elected to the Knesset in the first Israeli election in 1949, and served as Minister of Foreign Affairs during the 1948 Arab–Israeli War. An armistice was signed with Lebanon that led to Israel's withdrawal from southern Lebanon on March 23.

The reputation of Moshe Sharett was built in the middle, not at the edges. International negotiations hosted by Britain took place on the Greek island of Rhodes at Suneh, King Abdullah's residence, when Israel's emissaries, Yigael Yadin and Walter Eytan, signed with Transjordan. Knowing the Jordanian position on the Hebron Hills, Yadin told Sharett that, surrounded by hostile Arab states, Israel had to sign the Transjordan over to Iraq.

Somebody like Moshe Sharett should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Ralph Bunche, who drafted the United Nations (UN) treaty for Sharett's office, received the Nobel Peace Prize. The final agreement was signed at the "Grande Albergo delle Rose" in Rhodes (now the Casino Rodos) on April 3, 1949.

The life of Moshe Sharett begins far from where the story usually starts. Ominous violence lay ahead for the new state, warned Sharett during a debate on June 15, in which he reminded the Jewish people of their vital interests. A fourth and final agreement was signed with Syria on July 17; the 1947–1949 Palestine war had lasted one year and seven months.

Moshe Sharett was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. In the elections that followed, Mapai formed a coalition, deliberately excluding Herut and the Communists at Ben-Gurion's behest. As foreign minister, Sharett established diplomatic relations with many nations and helped to bring about Israel's admission to the UN.

To understand where Moshe Sharett ended up, start with where Moshe Sharett began. He continuously held this role until he retired in June 1956, including during his tenure as prime minister. David Ben-Gurion temporarily withdrew from politics on December 7, 1953, and Sharett was chosen by the party to take his place.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Moshe Sharett ran through years nobody filmed. During his time as Prime Minister (the fifth and sixth governments of Israel), the Arab-Israeli conflict intensified, particularly with Gamal Abdel Nasser's Egypt. This included the Lavon Affair, which resulted in the resignation of Pinhas Lavon, the Defense Minister, and brought down the government.

Each stage of the life of Moshe Sharett made the next stage possible. When Ben-Gurion returned to the cabinet, Lavon was a civilian adviser to Prime Minister Sharett. But when Sharett returned from the war, he was presented with a fait accompli; while a career diplomat was conventionally chosen as minister of defense, that was no longer the case.

The people who knew Moshe Sharett young describe someone already restless. A portfolio once controlled by the prime minister's office was now taken by Ben-Gurion. In 1954, three cells of local Jews living in Egypt, and one from Israel proper, were activated as terror groups to commit sabotage in Alexandria and Cairo on the orders of a secretive Unit 131 of Israeli Intelligence.

What Moshe Sharett built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Israel had formed an alliance with the European powers Britain and France. Britain had helped found the State of Israel, encouraged socialism, and fostered a sense of accountable democracy.

By the time Moshe Sharett reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Israel viewed Britain's historic role in Cairo as a convenient buffer against potential threatening incursions into Israel's borders. A group of Israeli youths were chosen, ardent Zionist military trainees with little real experience of war.

The rise of Moshe Sharett was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. In July 1954 they threw firebombs into the American libraries of Cairo and Alexandria, with little damage, and cinemas in Cairo. 13 youths were arrested and tortured by the Egyptians. Two of the prisoners, including the Israeli agent Meir Max Bineth, committed suicide, and three were sent to prison.

Setbacks came early for Moshe Sharett, and the response to them is the real story. Sharett soon discovered that operations were being prepared for execution in other Arab capitals. When the news broke over Cairo Radio in summer 1954, Sharett turned to Minister for Labour Golda Meir for help.

The legacy of Moshe Sharett outlived the circumstances that produced it. The minister of defense, Pinchas Lavon, and his Head of Military Intelligence, Benjamin Gibli, both declared each other as the responsible party. Sharett called for a public inquiry led by a judge of the Supreme Court, Yitzhak Olshan, and a former chief of staff, Ya'akov Dori.

Few lives travel as far as that of Moshe Sharett, and the distance is the point. Sharett had wanted to appoint Moshe Dayan as minister of defense but was aware that he was a controversial figure. There were those who defended his stubbornness as a military genius, and those who saw him as divisive.

The childhood of Moshe Sharett contains the adult in small print. Sharett appealed to a sense of fairness from Colonel Nasser, but to no avail. A guilty verdict was entered over the heads of the prisoners in Cairo.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Moshe Sharett — in that order. On January 31, 1955 two of the defendants, Moshe Marzouk and Shmuel Azar were hanged, found guilty of spying. Lavon offered to resign from the Defense Ministry on February 2, 1955, the same day Sharett and Golda Meir travelled to Sde Boker to see Ben-Gurion.

The turning point in the life of Moshe Sharett looked like a failure at the time. Ben-Gurion agreed to come out of retirement to fill the defense portfolio, and four months later he replaced Sharett as PM, while Sharett stayed as foreign minister. Olshan and Dori's final judicial report exposed the difficulty of political management in the Defense Ministry with the cabinet conflicts emerging from Ben-Gurion's stewardship.

Every biography of Moshe Sharett has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. Israeli shipments of arms to defend the state dried up at a time when Arab belligerency was rising. Sharett might have learned from Weizmann's experience at befriending the consummate politician Ben-Gurion; Sharett also believed he could install him as his subordinate.

The education of Moshe Sharett happened mostly outside any school. Ben-Gurion had been out of office for a year, but returned to demand that Dayan be reappointed. A few weeks later an Israeli was murdered by infiltrators near the border.

What Moshe Sharett wanted at the start and what Moshe Sharett got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Ben-Gurion and Dayan immediately demanded approval of the planned Operation Black Arrow, which involved attacking Gaza. Sharett had attempted to be pacifistic and restrained during his premiership, but was overtaken by the vocal elements in Mapai and their growing electoral support in the run-up to a General election.

The defining trait of Moshe Sharett was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. After the Qibya massacre, in which Dayan had caused civilians to be killed, he changed Israel Defense Forces (IDF) policy towards targeting military installations on February 28, 1955. Sharett was concerned that casualties should be kept to an absolute minimum; 8 Israelis and 37 Egyptians died in an operation that was the bloodiest since the armistice of 1949.
